Chapter 9: Becoming Notorious
It’s funny how life can surprise us, isn’t it? Ruth Bader Ginsburg never set out to become a cultural icon, much less one whose face would show up on T-shirts and murals all across the country. But as the years rolled on, that’s exactly what happened.
Suddenly, young people were wearing her image, artists were painting her into cityscapes, and the name “Notorious RBG” was showing up everywhere online—a clever play on her initials and the famous rapper, Notorious B.I.G. At first, Ruth laughed it off. She saw it as a bit of fun, something lighthearted. But deep down, she understood why it was happening.
There was something about Ruth that made people believe things could get better. She stood as living proof that when you hold onto your convictions and keep pushing forward, one person really can make a difference. And she didn’t shy away from this new spotlight. Instead, she leaned in—meeting with students, giving talks, and urging everyone to use their voices. She talked about why voting matters, why we have to stay informed, and why we should never give up on the promise of equality.
Through it all, Ruth’s humor sparkled. She’d make jokes about her tough workouts, her love for opera, and, of course, her famous collection of lace collars. Yes, she became a pop culture sensation, but she never lost focus on what truly mattered. She used her popularity as a chance to shine a light on issues that deserved attention—to remind people that the fight for justice is ongoing, and every voice counts.
For so many, Ruth became a guiding star—a beacon, really—showing us that change is possible, even when it feels far away. She inspired a whole new generation to believe in the power of law and, even more importantly, to believe in their own ability to shape the world around them.
